text: George Mesrop Avakian (Armenian: Ջորջ (Գևորգ) Ավագյան; Russian: Геворк Авакян; March 15, 1919 – November 22, 2017) was an American record producer, artist manager, writer, educator, and executive. He was a major force in the expansion and development of the U.S. recording industry from 1939 to the early 1960s, working at Decca Records, Columbia Records, World Pacific Records, Warner Bros. Records, and RCA Records. As an independent producer and manager from the 1960s to the early 2000s, he collaborated with artists such as Louis Armstrong, Miles Davis, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman, Dave Brubeck, Eddie Condon, Keith Jarrett, Erroll Garner, Buck Clayton, Sonny Rollins, Paul Desmond, Edith Piaf, Bob Newhart, Johnny Mathis, John Cage, Alan Hovhaness, Ravi Shankar, and many other notable jazz musicians and composers. Born in 1919 in Armavir, Russia, to Armenian parents Mesrop and Manoushak Avakian, he moved to the United States in July 1923 as a first-class passenger on the S/S Argentina from Trieste to New York. His younger brother was the photographer and filmmaker Aram Avakian (1926–1987). Avakian became a jazz fan in his early teens through radio listening, with early favorites including Duke Ellington, Fletcher Henderson, Fats Waller, the Casa Loma Orchestra, and Benny Goodman. He interviewed Goodman for the Horace Mann School Record during his senior year at Yale, beginning his extensive collection of jazz recordings and writing letters to companies like Decca and the American Record Corporation (ARC), which had acquired the catalogs of the bankrupt OKeh and Brunswick Records. While at Yale, Decca Records' Jack Kapp responded to his letters and hired him to produce Chicago Jazz (1940), featuring Eddie Condon, Jimmy McPartland, and George Wettling, which became the first "jazz album" and included a liner note essay with full credits and background, setting a template for future jazz releases. In 1940, during the swing era, CBS, having acquired ARC, formed Columbia Records and sought to feature jazz origins; after John Hammond declined the role, he recommended Avakian. In his third year at Yale, Avakian began researching and assembling the Hot Jazz Classics series at Columbia's Bridgeport vaults, creating boxed sets for Louis Armstrong, Bix Beiderbecke, Fletcher Henderson, Bessie Smith, and Billie Holiday, including many previously unreleased sides. He discovered unreleased Louis Armstrong Hot 5 and Hot 7 recordings while working on King Louis, forming a strong personal and professional friendship with Armstrong. After graduating from Yale, Avakian served in the U.S. Army and was recalled in 1944 for special training in European languages at Harvard; while stationed in Boston, he produced a jazz radio program for the Office of War Information featuring Eddie Condon, James P. Johnson, and Fletcher Henderson, and continued writing for Down Beat, Jazz Magazine, and Mademoiselle while in the Pacific. Post-war, he returned to Columbia Records, where he oversaw the Popular Music and International divisions, continuing the Hot Jazz Classics and Special Editions and Archives series, and was responsible for issuing the first 100 pop records in the 331⁄3rpm long-playing format, a new technology developed by Columbia. He also met his future wife, Anahid Ajemian (1925–2016), a violinist and sister to pianist Maro Ajemian (1921–1978), both of whom studied at the Institute of Musical Art (later Juilliard), launched careers at New York's Town Hall, and championed contemporary composers such as Aram Khatchaturian, John Cage, Alan Hovhaness, Lou Harrison, Ernst Krenek, and Elliott Carter. Avakian and Ajemian married in 1948 and remained married until Anahid's death in 2016. In 1948, Avakian taught one of the first academic jazz history courses at New York University and collaborated with Walter Schaap and Charles Delaunay on The New Hot Discography, an English translation and expansion of Delaunay's Hot Discography, the first significant catalog of existing jazz records. He financed the first recordings of John Cage and Alan Hovhaness (for Dial Records after the label shifted from bebop to classical) and was one of the co-founders of the National Association of Recording Arts and Sciences (NARAS, now The Recording Academy, presenters of the Grammy Awards) in 1957, serving as president from 1966 to 1967. At Columbia and later at Pacific Jazz, Warner Bros., RCA, and as an independent producer, Avakian worked with a wide range of artists, including Dave Brubeck, Erroll Garner, Mahalia Jackson, Ravi Shankar, Gil Evans, Lotte Lenya, Gerry Mulligan, Art Blakey, Buck Clayton, Eddie Condon, Tony Bennett, Edith Piaf, Johnny Mathis, and Frankie Yankovic. He signed Miles Davis and Dave Brubeck to the label, both of whom had previously recorded only for independents with limited distribution. Avakian was innovative in recording practices: he made Columbia the first major record company to record live performances of jazz and popular music, releasing a 2-LP set of Benny Goodman's 1938 Carnegie Hall concert in 1950 and recording Lionel Hampton, Harry James, and Louis Armstrong live. He also worked with Armstrong in the studio, producing some of his best later recordings, including Louis Armstrong Plays W. C. Handy (1954). From 1956 to 1963, he produced several landmark live Newport Jazz Festival albums, including Ellington at Newport (1956) and the companion album to the film Jazz On A Summer's Day (1958). He was among the first producers of popular music to fully embrace multitrack recording and tape editing, overdubbing Louis Armstrong on the best-selling single "Mack The Knife" in 1955 and overdubbing and editing Miles Davis's Miles Ahead in 1957. In 1958, after a groundbreaking 12-year run at Columbia, he left to co-found a record company for Warner Bros., the only major film studio without its own label at the time, alongside former colleague Jim Conkling. There, he signed Bob Newhart, producing the first comedy album to win a Best Album Grammy Award, and also signed the Everly Brothers and Bill Haley & His Comets. He personally financed and produced the first three albums by Alan Hovhaness and John Cage, and in 1958 presented The 25-Year Retrospective Concert of the Music of John Cage at Town Hall, which he also recorded and sold independently. The year before, Avakian and Ajemian produced a three-concert series at Town Hall titled Music For Moderns, featuring jazz musicians and modern composers, including Anahid Ajemian, Dimitri Mitropoulos, the Duke Ellington Orchestra, the Modern Jazz Quartet, Mahalia Jackson, Chico Hamilton, composers Virgil Thomson and Carlos Surinach, pianist William Masselos, violist Walter Trampler, and opera baritone Martial Singher. In 1960, Avakian left Warner Bros. to join RCA as manager of popular artists and repertoire, working again with jazz musicians such as Lambert, Hendricks, and Bavan, Paul Desmond, Sonny Rollins (signed for an unprecedented sum), Gary Burton, and Benny Goodman. In 1962, he planned and accompanied Benny Goodman on a landmark tour of the USSR, gaining valuable experience with Russian music that proved useful in the following years. By late 1962, Avakian felt the pressure of managing a record label and negotiated an independent production deal with RCA, working on a per-project basis. He also began managing and producing his own artists, including John Lewis and Gunther Schuller's Orchestra U.S.A., singer/songwriter Bob Morrison, and saxophonist Charles Lloyd. Though best known for jazz and pop album production, Avakian was involved in two theater projects: in 1947, he arranged for musicians led by Eddie Barefield to perform incidental music for A Streetcar Named Desire during its Philadelphia and Broadway runs; in 1965, he was an associate producer of the first Off-Broadway revival of Marc Blitzstein's The Cradle Will Rock and personally financed the recording of its cast album, the first complete recording of the show. Avakian promoted intercultural exchange between the U.S. and the Soviet Union; he was the first to record Soviet and American artists together (Pavel Lisitsian Sings Armenian Songs With Maro Ajemian At The Piano, New York Records, recorded in 1957, released in 1960). After organizing the Benny Goodman 1962 tour and Charles Lloyd's 1967 Tallinn Jazz Festival performance, he helped Duke Ellington and the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis orchestras plan their Soviet visits, befriending Russian music figures such as Leonid Pereverzev, Oleg Lundstrem, and Valery Ponomarev. He sponsored the first performance by Soviet musicians in the United States at the Village Gate in 1988 and arranged for the Branford Marsalis Quartet to play at the Moscow International Jazz Festival in 1990, marking the debut of American performers at that event. For his lifelong efforts, the Soviet Composers Union awarded him the Order of Lenin in 1990, the former Soviet Union's highest honor. From the 1970s to the 2000s, Avakian continued occasional record production, managing Helen Merrill and Datevik Hovanesian in the 1980s, and in the 1990s and 2000s, Sony Legacy consulted him for reissues of Miles Davis and Louis Armstrong albums and compilations. He remained active in jazz research and writing, discovering several previously unknown Louis Armstrong compositions at the Library of Congress, and in 1997 produced performances and a recording by trumpeter Randy Sandke and others (The Re-Discovered Louis and Bix, on Nagel-Heyer Records, 2000). In 2014, Avakian and Anahid Ajemian donated their extensive collection of jazz recordings and memorabilia to the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts at Lincoln Center; a major exhibit titled Music for Moderns: The Partnership of George Avakian and Anahid Ajemian was held there in 2016. After semi-retirement, he became involved in harness racing, owning and breeding several racehorses, including the champion pacer Presidential Ball. Avakian died on November 22, 2017, at the age of 98 at his home on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. The Avakians had three children: Maro, Anahid, and Gregory. He is a founding officer of the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (presenters of the Grammy Awards).
